newsitem.title: USA: Ford ends year with strong December sales.
newsitem.headline: Ford ends year with strong December sales.

text.p: Ford Motor Co., bucking the year-end softness experienced by most other automakers, said Monday its December U.S. sales rose 10.6 percent over a year earlier as truck sales surged ahead.

Ford's year-end rally capped off a flat sales year for the world's second-largest automaker, with total U.S. car and light truck sales up 0.5 percent to 3.84 million units from 3.8 million units in 1995.

The Ford results and an 8.2 percent December sales decline reported by Honda Motor Co. Ltd. brought industrywide U.S. car and light truck sales for 1996 to 15.14 million units -- a 1.9 percent increase from the 14.77 million sold in 1995.
The industry's U.S. sales performance in 1996 matched the 15.1 million light vehicles sold in the United States during 1994, which had been the highest annual total since 1988.
"Throughout 1996, the two hottest segments of the automotive market have been full-size pickups and sport utility vehicles," Ford sales and marketing chief Robert Rewey said in a statement.
"Every indication is that these segments will continue their dynamic growth and we're confident that, within them, Ford products will remain dominant by any criterion," he said.
Ford sold a record 2.15 million trucks in 1996, but it had tough competition from Chrysler Corp. trucks, Jeeps and minivans.
After steadily gaining U.S. vehicle market share over the past several years, Ford's share dipped slightly in 1996, to 25.4 percent from 25.8 percent in 1995.

The big market share winner for the year was Chrysler, which increased its share to 16.2 percent from 14.7 percent in 1995. Chrysler's sales for the year rose 12.5 percent to a record 2.45 million vehicles.

General Motors Corp.'s share of the market continued its steady decline in 1996, falling to 31.3 percent from 32.6 percent in 1995 and 33 percent in 1994. GM's total sales for the year fell 2.7 percent to 4.74 million cars and light trucks.

Honda and Toyota Motor Corp. continued their relentless drive for market share, with Toyota adding nearly 0.4 percentage point to 7.7 percent of the market -- a significant gain in an industry that hotly contests every tenth of a point of market share.
Honda ended the year with a 5.5 percent sales increase to 843,928 cars and trucks. Honda's market share increased to 5.6 percent from 5.3 percent a year earlier.
During the month of December, U.S. light vehicle sales totaled 1,127,204 vehicles, down 4 percent from the 1,174,578 sold in December 1995.

The seasonally adjusted annual sales rate for the month was 14.5 million units, down from 15.9 million units a year earlier and 14.9 million for the month of November 1996. The rate is calculated with seasonal factors supplied by the Commerce Department.

Ford's Taurus sedan retained its hotly contested status as the best selling car in the United States during 1996 for the fifth year in a row, with sales totaling 401,049 units, an increase of 9 percent over 1995. The nearest passenger car competitor was Honda's Accord, which recorded sales of 382,298 units.
Analysts estimate, however, that as much as half of all Tauruses are sold to daily rental fleets, so among actual consumers, the Accord far outsells the Taurus.
Ford Division General Manager Ross Roberts said he expected a closer race for the best selling car next year with the Accord.
Roberts, speaking to reporters, said he expected Taurus sales for 1997 to fall to 380,000 to 390,000 units.
He said much of the outcome of this year's contest will depend on how many Accords Honda can produce in the United States and how many it chooses to import from Japan.
"It will be close. We're not going to by any means give it to them," Roberts said.
He said in 1997 the Ford Division planned to focus on boosting sales of its entire lineup of vehicles. "I'd rather have five of the top 10 than the No. 1 selling car," he said.
Roberts added that the $1,000 rebate on the Taurus is not expected to change in the first quarter of 1997.
